rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabbat means she was destroyed; tabāb can also mean loss that leads to destruction.
rows.anchor: فإن التباب الهلاك ومنه قولهم أشابة أم تابة أهالكة من الهرم والعجز أو خسرت فإن التباب أيضا خسران يؤدي إلى الهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lahab is a flame or its heat; Abu Lahab was ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā’s kunya, explained by his rosy, fiery cheeks or wealth, not a son named Lahab.
rows.anchor: تسكن الهاء كنية عبد العز بن عبد المطلب لجماله أو لماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the command to warn his nearest kin, the Prophet called Quraysh to Ṣafā, asked whether they would believe a warning of an approaching army, and then warned them of the Hour.
rows.anchor: لما روى أنه لما نزل وأنذر عشيرتك الأقربين رقى رسول الله عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab answered with a curse and seized a stone to throw at the Prophet, but God prevented him from doing so.
rows.anchor: فقال عمه أبو لهب تبا لك يعني هلاكت باد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording about Abu Lahab’s hands is literal because he tried to throw a stone; describing them as destroyed is apt, while loss rebuts his belief that harming the Prophet profited him.
rows.anchor: فلا كناية في ذكر اليدين ووجه وصف يديه بالهلاك ظاهر وأما

rows.speaker: الماتريدي
rows.claim: Al-Māturīdī says Abu Lahab expected favors from both Muhammad and Quraysh; his hands lost their supposed gain through his defiance and Quraysh’s eventual defeat.
rows.anchor: وذكر في التأويلات ألما تريدية إنه كان كثير الإحسان إلى رسول الله عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “And he perished” reports the certain result after the first statement; the past tense marks an outcome that is assured.
rows.anchor: أي وهلك كله فهو أخبار بعد أخبار والتعبير بالماضي لتحقق وقوعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes the first line as destruction of Abu Lahab’s whole person, using “hand” for the self, as in the warning against casting oneself into ruin.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد بالأولى هلاك جملته كقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view treats both clauses as imprecations, indicating that Abu Lahab deserved a curse for destruction; a reported reading with qad instead marks fact rather than prayer.
rows.anchor: وقيل كلاهما دعاء عليه بالهلاك والمراد بيان استحقاقه لأن يدعى عليه بالهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kunya is not honorific: it may avoid his ugly idolatrous name or, more pointedly, call him a man of Hell because his name evokes flame.
rows.anchor: أو لكراهة ذكر اسمه القبيح إذ فيه إضافة إلى الصنم أو للتعريض بكونه جهنميا لأنه سيصلى نارا ذات لهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Itqān says Abu Lahab is the Quran’s only person identified by a kunya; the commentary explains that his personal name ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā is religiously forbidden.
rows.anchor: قال في الاتقان ليس في القرآن من الكنى غير أبي لهب ولم يذكر اسمه وهو عبد العزى أي الصنم لأنه حرام شرعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab had boasted that, if his nephew were right, his money and children would ransom him; his hope failed.
rows.anchor: إن كان ما يقول ابن أخي حقا فأنا افتدى منه نفسي بمالي وولدي فاستخلص منه وقد خاب رجاه وما حصل ما تمناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Utbah, Abu Lahab’s son and the Prophet’s former son-in-law, insulted him, spat toward him, and divorced his daughter; the Prophet prayed that a beast would attack Utbah.
rows.anchor: فأتاه فقال يا محمد هو كافر بالنجم إذا هوى وبالذي دنا فتدلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A lion killed Utbah in Syria after Abu Lahab, fearing the Prophet’s prayer, gathered Quraysh around his son; a monk had warned that the area was full of lions.
rows.anchor: فأشرف عليهم راهب من الدير فقال إن هذه أرض مسبعة فقال أبو لهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab died of al-ʿadasah, a usually fatal boil resembling plague, seven nights after Badr; his family avoided the body for fear of contagion.
rows.anchor: وهلك أبو لهب بالعدسة بعد وقعة بدر لسبع ليال والعدسة بثرة تخرج في البدن تشبه العدسة وهي من جنس الطاعون تقتل غالبا فاجتنبه أهله مخافة العدوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accounts differ on the burial: some say hired men leaned the corpse against a wall and piled stones behind it; another says they pushed it into a grave from afar with a stick.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية حفروا له ثم دفعوه بعود في حفرته وقذفوه بالحجارة

rows.speaker: عائشة رضي الله عنها
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reportedly covered her face whenever she passed the place where Abu Lahab was buried.
rows.anchor: إنها كانت إذا مرت بموضعه ذلك غطت وجهها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stoned grave outside al-Shubayka is not Abu Lahab’s; it belongs to two men who defiled the Kaaba and were crucified there in Abbasid times.
rows.anchor: والقبر الذي يرجم خارج باب الشبيكة الآن ليس بقبر أبي لهب وإنما هو قبر رجلين لطخا الكعبة بالعذرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The announced punishment is his certain fate in this life and the next: he will enter a blazing fire.
rows.anchor: أي ما ذكر من العذاب مآل أمره في النشأة الأولى وفي النشأة الآخرة سيدخل لا محالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire is immense, burning Hellfire.
rows.anchor: نارا عظيمة ذات اشتعال وتوقد وهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse does not prove Abu Lahab could never believe: entry into fire may follow sin rather than disbelief, so the verse need not create a command to believe he would remain faithless.
rows.anchor: ولسي هذا نصا في إنه لا يؤمن أبدا حتى يلزم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab’s wife was Umm Jamīl, sister of Abū Sufyān and aunt of Muʿāwiya; she was also called al-ʿAwrāʾ.
rows.anchor: وهي أم جميل بنت حرب بن أمية أخت أبي سفاين عمة معاوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umm Jamīl carried thorny brush at night and spread it on the Prophet’s path; another tafsir says she and her actions caused hardship for him and his companions.
rows.anchor: وكانت تحمل حزمة من الشوك والحسك والسعدان فتنشرها بالليل في طريق النبي عليه السلام

rows.speaker: الكاشفي
rows.claim: Al-Kāshifī says she laid thorns along the Prophet’s way when he went to prayer, while he gently questioned what sort of neighborly conduct this was.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير الكاشفي وآن حضرت كه بنماز بيرون آمدي آنها برسرراه بركرفتي وبطريق ملايمت كفتى اين ه نوع همسا يكيست

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī favors the accusative as a term of insult or blame, a reading that lets the speaker disparage Umm Jamīl.
rows.anchor: ونصب حمالة على الشتم والذم أي أذم حمالة الحطب قال الزمخشري وأنا استحب هذه القراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative parses the phrase as a circumstantial description: she will carry fuel of Hell such as zaqqūm and ḍarīʿ, with a fire chain around her neck, as fitting recompense.
rows.anchor: وقيل على الحالية بناه على أن الإضافة غر حقيقية إذا المراد إنها تحمل يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says she carried wood on her back despite her wealth because of extreme miserliness, so the accusative is necessarily blame.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة إنها مع كثرة مالها تحمل الحطب على ظرها لشدة بخلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that she carried fuel between people by spreading slander and kindling hostility.
rows.anchor: وقيل كانت تمشي بالنميمة وتفسد بين الناس تحمل الحطب بينهم أي توقد بينهم النائرة وتورث الشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Persian idiom “wood carrier” describes malicious speech that sets conflict between two people alight.
rows.anchor: هيزم كشى عبارتست ازسخن ينى كه آتش خصومت ميان دوكس برمى افروزد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jīd means neck, its collar, or its front; masad is rope tightly twisted from fiber, leather, or other material.
rows.anchor: والجيد بالكسر العنق ومقلده أو مقدمه كما في

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatically the clause is circumstantial; she ties the thorn bundle to her neck like a wood carrier, humiliating her despite her household’s high status and wealth.
rows.anchor: وإنها تحمل تلك الحزمة من الشوك وتربطها في جيدها كما يفعل الحطابون تخسيسا حالها وتصويرا لها بصورة بعض الحطابات

rows.speaker: مرة الهمداني
rows.claim: Murra al-Hamdānī says she daily laid thorns on the Muslims’ path; one night an angel pulled the rope as she rested, strangling her and sending her to Hell.
rows.anchor: قال مرة الهمداني كانت أم جميل تأتي كل يوم بابالة من حسك فتطرحها على طريق المسلمين فبينما هي ذات ليلة حاملة حزمة أعيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report in Yanbūʿ al-Ḥayāt says she confronted Abū Sufyān over the sura; a snake protected the Prophet, and she later died in unbelief while her brother became Muslim.
rows.anchor: وفي ينبوع الحياة إنها لما بلغها سورة تبت يدا أبي لهب جاءت إلى أخيها أبي سفيان في بيته وهي متحرقة غضبي

rows.speaker: كشف الأسرار
rows.claim: Kashf al-Asrār compares outwardly religious Balʿam to the cave dog: outward appearance cannot erase the primordial decree of wretchedness or felicity.
rows.anchor: سك أصحاب الكهف رنك كفزادشت ولباس بلعام باعور طراز دين داشت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recitation convention pauses after min masad and then adds the takbīr previously discussed.
rows.anchor: قوله من مسد بالوقف يعني يوقف عليه ثم يجاء بالتكبير لما مر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura is described as four or five verses and as either Meccan or Medinan.
rows.anchor: أربع أو خمس آيات مكية أو مدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He” may be the pronoun of the affair, with the following sentence explaining it; the opening creates emphasis through initial ambiguity and explanation.
rows.anchor: الضمير للشأن كقولك هو زيد منطلق وارتفاعه بالابتداء وخبره الجملة ولا حاجة إلى العائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “He” refers to the deity about whom the questioners asked; the sura answers their request to describe God and state His lineage by denying parentage and likeness.
rows.anchor: إذ روى إن المشركين قالوا للنبي عليه السلام

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī’s preferred parsing takes “Allah” as predicate and “Aḥad” as an appositive to it; apposition of an indefinite to a definite is allowed when informative.
rows.anchor: فالضمير حينئذ مبتدأوخبره واحد بدل منه وإبدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement is comprehensive evidence for the true God and gathers the meanings of the beautiful names.
rows.anchor: دال على الإله الحق دلالة جامعة لمعاني الأسماء الحسنى كلها

rows.speaker: القاشاني
rows.claim: Al-Qāshānī says “He” names the Divine Essence as it is in itself, absolute and true with all, some, or none of the names considered.
rows.anchor: هو عندنا اسم الذات الإلهية من حيث هي هي أي المطلقة الصادق عليها مع جميعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is the servant who realizes all divine names and ranks highest through the Greatest Name; this designation belongs in truth to him and, by following him, perfect inheritors.
rows.anchor: وعبد الله هو العبد الذي تحلى بجميع أسمائه فلا يكون في عباده أرفع مقاما وأعلى شأنا منه لتحققه بالاسم الأعظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥad denotes the Essence alone without multiplicity or relation, while wāḥid denotes the Essence considered with the multiplicity of attributes and therefore relates to creation.
rows.anchor: والأحد اسم لمن لا يشاركه شيء في ذاته كما أن الواحد اسم لمن لا يشاركه شيء في صفاته يعني أن الأحد هو الذات وحدها بلا اعتبار كثرة فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human knowledge of God concerns the relation between Him and creation; perfected knowers still admit that some knowledge exceeds human capacity, and essential oneness belongs truly to God.
rows.anchor: العلم الإلهي هو العلم بالحق من حيث الارتباط بينه وبين الخلق وانتشاء العالم منه بقدر الطاقة البشرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servant of al-Aḥad is the unique pole of his age at the station of supreme oneness; the servant of al-Wāḥid reaches the station of unity and perceives the unity of the names.
rows.anchor: وعبد الأحد هو وحيد الوقت صاحب الزمان الذي له القطبية الكبرى والقيام بالأحدية الأولى وعبد الواحد هو الذي بلغه الله الحضرة الواحدية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit denial of begetting refutes claims about angels and Jesus; the past tense states that no child issued from God, since He has no consort of His kind and needs no helper or successor.
rows.anchor: تنصيصا على إبطال زعم المفترين في حق الملائكة والمسيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording differs from 17:111 because some Christians claim Jesus is literally God’s son, while others say God adopted him as an honorific; each phrase refutes one claim.
rows.anchor: منهم من قال عيسى ولد الله حقيقة فقوله لم يلد إشارة إلى الرد عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Was not begotten” denies any source of God’s existence, since He cannot be preceded by nonexistence.
rows.anchor: أي لم يصدر عن شيء لاستحالة نسبة العدم إليه سابقا أولا حقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some argue that parenthood and begetting entail likeness, but God’s necessary identity cannot resemble contingent identities.
rows.anchor: الوالدية والمولودية لا تكونان إلا بالمثلية فإن المولود لا بد أن يكون مثل الوالد

rows.speaker: البقلي
rows.claim: Al-Baqlī interprets the phrase as saying God is not the locus of temporal events and temporal events are not His locus.
rows.anchor: وقال البقلي لم يلد ولم يولد أي لم يكن هو محل الحوادث ولا الحوادث محله

rows.speaker: كشف الأسرار
rows.claim: Kashf al-Asrār explains that “He did not beget” comes first because some unbelievers claimed God had a child, while none claimed He was born.
rows.anchor: قدم ذكر لم يلد لأن من الكفار من ادعى إن له ولدا ولم يدع أحد إنه مولود

rows.speaker: التفسير الفارسي
rows.claim: The Persian commentary assigns the denial of begetting to refuting Jews about ʿUzayr and the denial of being born to refuting Christians about Jesus.
rows.anchor: لم يلد رد يهوداست كه كفتند عزيز سر اوست ولم يولد رد نصارى است

rows.speaker: أبو الليث
rows.claim: Abū al-Layth says God has no child to inherit from Him and no parent from whom to inherit dominion.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الليث لم يلد يعني لم يكن له ولد يرثه ولم يولد يعني لم يكن له والد يرث ملكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kufuwan means an equal or likeness; moving “to Him” ahead emphasizes that no one matches God, and it may also deny a spouse. The delayed subject preserves the rhyme, while the three denials exclude every kind of peer.
rows.anchor: يقال هذا كفاؤه وكفؤه مثله وكافأ فلانا ماثله وله صلة لكفؤا قدمت عليه مع أن حقها التأخر عنه للاهتمام بها

rows.speaker: القاشاني
rows.claim: Al-Qāshānī says the Divine Essence admits neither multiplicity nor division; nothing equals pure existence because everything besides absolute existence is sheer nonexistence.
rows.anchor: ما كانت هويته الأحية غير قابلة للكثرة والانقسام ولم تكن مقارنة الوحدة الذاتية

rows.speaker: الكاشفي
rows.claim: Al-Kāshifī says the final verse rebuts Magians and Arab polytheists who alleged a counterpart; each answer in the sura answers the question raised by the preceding answer.
rows.anchor: رد مجوس ومشركان عربست كه كفتند اورا كفوهست نعوذ بالله وكفته اند هر آيتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some assign successive spiritual audiences to the phrases: “He” for bewildered lovers, “Allah” for monotheists, “Aḥad” for gnostics, al-Ṣamad for scholars, and “He did not beget” for the wise.
rows.anchor: كاشف الوالهين بقوله هو وكاشف الموحدين بقوله الله وكاشف العارفين بقوله أحد

rows.speaker: بعض الكبار
rows.claim: Some great Sufis read the sura as describing the state of descent or attraction, beginning with “He is Allah, One,” though the surviving passage breaks off mid-explanation.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الكبار إن سورة الإخلاص إشارة إلى حال النزول وهو حال المجذوب فأولا يقول هو الله أحد الله الصمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falaq means dawn, split from the night; the word is understood as a passive result, since dawn emerges when its covering darkness is split away.
rows.anchor: الفلق الصبح لأنه يفلق عنه الليل ويفرق فهو من باب الحذف والإيصال فعل بمعنى مفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falaq can also mean creation: all possible things were hidden beneath nonexistence until God split that darkness by bringing them into being.
rows.anchor: والفلق أيضا الخلق لأن الممكنات بأسرها كانت أعيانا ثابتة في علم الله مستورة تحت ظلمة العدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking refuge in the Lord of dawn promises deliverance from darkness, constriction, and distress, encouraging the seeker to persist in asking for protection.
rows.anchor: وفي تعليق العياذ باسم الرب المضاف إلى الفلق المبنىء عن النور عقيب الظلمة والسعة بعد الضيق والفتق بعد الرتق عدة كريمة بإعادة العائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People say heaviness and grief give way to lightness and joy when dawn rises.
rows.anchor: قالوا إذا طلع الصبح تتبدل الثقلة بالخفة والغم بالسرور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Joseph’s knee hurt in the well; near dawn Gabriel taught him to pray, and God relieved his distress. Joseph then prayed for all afflicted people, who find some easing late at night.
rows.anchor: روى أن يوسف عليه السلام لما ألقى في الجب وجعت ركبته وجعا شديدا فبات ليلته ساهرا فلما قرب طلوع الصبح نزل جبريل

rows.speaker: بعض الصحابة
rows.claim: An unnamed Companion in Syria saw non-Muslims living comfortably and said he did not mind because the Hellfire’s “fālaq” awaited them; it is a house that makes Hell’s inhabitants cry when opened.
rows.anchor: وعن بعض الصحابة رضي الله عنهم إنه قدم الشأم فرأى دور أهل الذمة وما هم فيه من خفض العيش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refuge covers harm from every created kind, including humans, jinn, beasts, and vermin.
rows.anchor: أي من شر ما خلقه من الثقلين وغيرهم كائنا ما كان من ذوات الطبائع والاختيار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase includes bodily and other harm, such as assault, killing, insult, bites, stings, and sorcery; evil is tied to the material world’s mixture and conflicting qualities, while the realm of command is pure good.
rows.anchor: فيشمل جميع الشرور والمضار بدنية كانت أو غيرها من ضرب وقتل وشتم وعض ولدغ وسحر ونحوها وءافة الشر إليه لاختصاصه بعالم الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Muʿtazilites read min sharrin mā khalaq with an implied negation to deny that God created evil; the commentary rejects this reading as resting on a false doctrine, since God created everything.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض المعتزلة القائلين بأن الله لم يخلق الشر من شر بالتنوين ما خلق على النفي وهي قراء مردودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night is singled out although included in all created evils because danger is frequent then, the need for refuge is acute, and naming a particular danger stresses the plea.
rows.anchor: تخصيص لبعض الشرور بالذكر مع اندارجه فيما قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghāsiq is the deeply dark night after twilight; the cited verse and lexicon explain it as darkness gathering or intensifying, with the root also used for an eye filled with or shedding tears.
rows.anchor: أي ومن شر ليل مختلط ظلامه مشتد وذلك بعد غيبوبة الشفق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The danger is attributed to night because it occurs then; waqaba means entering its hollow or disappearing, and the qualifier marks when darkness penetrates everything and harm becomes harder to avoid.
rows.anchor: وإضافة الشر إلى الليل لملابسته له بحدوثه فيه وتنكيره لعدم شمول الشر لجميع أفراده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proverbs call night more concealing and treacherous because ambush, crime, and harm multiply when darkness makes help scarce; a legal example contrasts the rule for killing an armed attacker at night and by day.
rows.anchor: ولذلك قيل الليل أخفى للويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic instructions to avoid setting out early at night, cover vessels, close doors, secure waterskins, and gather children are precautions against nighttime harm.
rows.anchor: ونهى رسول الله عليه السلام ، عن السير في أول الليل

rows.speaker: عائشة رضي الله عنها
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet pointed to the moon and told her to seek refuge from its harm, interpreting it as the “ghāsiq when it enters.” Its harms include bodily affliction and religious temptation to worship celestial bodies.
rows.anchor: إنها قالت أخذ رسول الله علي السلام بيدي فأشار إلى القمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views identify the moon at its eclipse or waning, when sorcery and illness were thought more likely, or the Pleiades when setting, associated with plague and disease; another broad reading is any evil that attacks.
rows.anchor: وقيل التعبير عن القمر بالغاسق لأن جرمه مظلم وإنما يستنير بضوء الشمس ووقوبه المحاق في آخر الشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafth is a breath-like blowing without saliva, unlike taffl, which includes saliva; the commentary records two vowelings of the verb.
rows.anchor: من النفث وهو شبه النفخ يكون في الرقية ولا ريق معه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled form naffāthāt suggests repeated, habitual action; the undoubled form may denote a single act or repetition.
rows.anchor: والنفاثات بالشديد يراد منها تكرار الفعل والاحتراف به والنفاثات تكون للدفعة الواحدة من الفعل ولتكراره أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knots are tied in string, cord, or hair while the sorcerer blows and recites; the term derives from a binding resolve, hence the sorcerer is called a knotter.
rows.anchor: جمع عقدة وهي ما يعده الساحر على وتر أو حبل أو شعر وهو ينفث ويرقى وأصله من العزيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means the evil of sorcerers, especially women who tie knots and blow on them; its definite form may point to known practitioners or encompass all such women.
rows.anchor: والمعنى ومن شر النفوس أو النساء السواحر اللاتي يعقدن عقدا في خيوط وينفثن عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The named practitioners were Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam and his daughters; the spell used the Prophet’s comb hairs, was hidden in a well, and left him ill for six months.
rows.anchor: وتولاه لبيد بن أعصم اليهودي وبناته وهن النفاثات في العقد فدفنها في بئر أريس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel disclosed the spell’s place, maker, and materials; ʿAlī, al-Zubayr, and ʿAmmār drained the well and retrieved comb teeth and eleven knotted cords, which the Prophet recited over until the knots loosened and he recovered.
rows.anchor: فأرسل عليه السلام عليا والزبير وعمارا رضي الله عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report supports ruqya using God’s words or the Prophet’s words, but the commentary forbids trusting spells in Hebrew, Syriac, or Hindi; the Prophet declined to kill the culprit to avoid stirring wider harm.
rows.anchor: فلذا جوز الاسترقاء بما كان من كلام الله وكلام رسوله لا بما كان بالعبرية والسريانية والهندية

rows.speaker: عائشة رضي الله عنها
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha says the Prophet never took personal revenge; he became angry only over God’s sanctity, when God would punish.
rows.anchor: قالت عائشة رضي الله عنها ما غضب النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A figurative interpretation takes knot-blowing as undermining men’s resolve through manipulative tricks; women’s influence turns men from one judgment to another, so refuge is sought from their harm.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد بالنفث في العقد إبطال عزائم الرجال بالحيل مستعار من تليين العقدة بنفث الريق ليسهل حلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Lord of people owns their affairs and nurtures them by providing what benefits them and warding off harm.
rows.anchor: أي مالك أمورهم ومربيهم بإفاضة ما يصلحهم ودفع ما يضرهم

rows.speaker: القاشاني
rows.claim: Al-Qāshānī says the Lord of people is the Essence considered with all attributes, since the human being gathers the levels of existence.
rows.anchor: رب الناس هو الذات مع جميع الصفات لأن الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sura seeks refuge in God’s Essence after the earlier refuge in an attribute, al-Hādī; the sequence moves from attributes toward the Essence.
rows.anchor: تعوذ بوجهه بعد ما تعوذ بصفاته ولهذا تأخرت هذه الصورة عن المعوذة الأولى إذ فيها تعوذ في مقام الصفات باسمه الهادي فهداه إلى ذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophetic prayer progresses from seeking refuge in God’s pleasure and pardon to seeking refuge in God Himself; scholars differ over the order of the first two pleas.
rows.anchor: ابتدأ بالتعوذ بالرضى الذي هو من الصفات لقرب الصفات من الذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One who still attends to things besides God seeks protection through His acts and attributes; the fully immersed monotheist seeks refuge only in God, as the Prophet’s final plea does.
rows.anchor: من بقى له التفات إلى غير الله استعاذ بأفعال الله وصفاته فأما من توغل في بحر التوحيد بحيث لا يرى في الوجود إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing appeal to God signals that all affairs return to Him; it also hints at humanity’s forgotten primordial covenant, which would otherwise have kept people continually in God’s care.
rows.anchor: ففي الالتجاء إلى الله في هذه السورة دلالة على ختم الأمر فإن الله تعالى هو الأول الآخر وإليه يرجع الأمر كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “King of people” clarifies that God’s nurture is full sovereignty and comprehensive control, unlike a human master’s limited rule by force or politics; no creaturely comparison limits God’s ownership.
rows.anchor: لك الحمد لا إله إلا أنت رب كل شيء ومليكه ولم يرد ومالكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary prefers Malik to Mālik here: prophetic supplication uses “King,” independent divine names precede attached ones, and God’s final declaration of sovereignty confirms the stronger title; it avoids repeating rabb, while Malik is also preferred in al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: وأيضا فالأسماء المستقلة لها تقدم على الأسماء المضافة واسم الملك ورد مستقلا بخلاف المالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God of people” says His rule is grounded in true divinity and worship, not mere administration: as deity He has complete power to give life, cause death, create, and annihilate.
rows.anchor: هو لبيان إن ملكه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the mystical reading, kingship signifies annihilation in God, divinity subsistence through God; after the servant returns to existence and worship, seeking refuge from whispering becomes possible because it requires a receptive existent locus.
rows.anchor: وأيضا إن ملك الناس إشارة إلى حال الفناء في الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three presences correspond to Rabb, Malik, and Ilah and to spiritual leaders: the two imams serve the pole, while the pole alone has unrestricted unveiling; their access to the unseen and visible realms differs.
rows.anchor: وأيضا مقام الربوبية المقيدة بالناس هو لحضرة الامام الذي على باب عالم الملكوت

rows.speaker: الإرشاد
rows.claim: Al-Irshād explains that “people” are specified because they are the intended targets of Satan; affirming their servitude and divine ownership alludes to rescue from his dominion.
rows.anchor: تخصيص الإضافة بالناس مع انتظام جميع العالمين في سلك ربوبيته تعالى وملكوته وألوهيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “people” provides clarification and emphasis; repeating a noble subject is fitting, and a poet compares repeated remembrance of Nuʿmān to fragrance that grows stronger.
rows.anchor: وتكرير المضاف إليه لمزيد الكشف والتقرير بالإضافة فإن ما لا شرف فيه لا يعبأ به ولا يعاد ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waswās names a hidden, imperceptible whisper or the whispering itself; the commentary distinguishes a verbal noun from an event noun by whether an act’s relation to agent and recipient is considered.
rows.anchor: هو اسم بمنى الوسوسة وهو الصوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form evokes repetition, since a whisperer persistently presses speech on a listener; waswās therefore names Satan through his recurring, subtle suggestions.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت الوسوسة كلاما يكرره الموسوس ويؤكده عند من يليه إليه كرر لفظها بإزاء تكرير معناها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan quietly urges sin by suggesting that God’s mercy is limitless or that there is plenty of time to repent; the refuge asks protection from his whole evil, not whispering alone.
rows.anchor: لأنه يدعو إلى المعصية بكلام خفي يفهمه القلب من غير أن يسمع صوته وذلك بالأغرار بسعة رحمة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description names Satan’s most harmful and pervasive trait. Refuge is sought through God’s name because Satan opposes the Merciful and takes on human forms and names; other attributes alone do not suffice.
rows.anchor: وإنما وصفه بأعظم فاته وأشدها شرا وأقواها تأثيرا وأعمها فسادا وإنما استعاذ منه بالإله دون بعض أسمائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first refuge addresses concealment and misguidance through the Lord of dawn, while this one appeals to the Lord of people against Satan.
rows.anchor: فلهذا لما تعوذ من الاحتجاب والضلالة تعوذ برب الفلق وههنا تعوذ برب الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic report says Satan cannot imitate the Prophet; the commentary extends this protection to perfected followers as manifestations of guidance.
rows.anchor: من رآني فقد رآني فإن الشيطان لا يتمثل بي وكذا لا يتمثل بصور الكمل من أمته

rows.speaker: بعض الكبار
rows.claim: Some spiritual authorities divide inspirations into true, God-given knowledge and insight, or angelic prompting that encourages obedience and benefit.
rows.anchor: قال بعض الكبار : الإلقاء إما صحيح أو فاسد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A saint asked God to show him Satan’s whispering and saw a human body like crystal, a black hollow behind the shoulders, and a pig-like tempter inserting its trunk near the heart; remembrance made it retreat, explaining khannās.
rows.anchor: إن بعض الأولياء سأل الله تعالى أن يريه كيف يأتي الشيطان ويوسوس فأراه الحق تعالى هيكل الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s cupping between the shoulders weakened Satan’s material and narrowed his ambush; the seal of prophethood there signified protection from whispers, while Adam’s companion did not submit.
rows.anchor: ولهذا السر الإلهي كان عليه السلام ، يحتجم بين كتفيه ويأمر بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan can enter bodies as a subtle body; his fiery origin does not make him burn because mixing with air yields a distinct composition, like the human body.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يدخل الشيطان في الأجسام لأنه جسم لطيف وهو وإن كان مخلوقا في الأصل من نار لكنه ليس بمحرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an inward reading, waswās points to sensory and imaginative powers, while khannās denotes the estimative faculty that supports reasoning through premises but retreats at the conclusion and revives doubt.
rows.anchor: وفي الوسواس إشارة إلى الوسواس الحاصل من القوة الحسية والخيالية وفي الخناس إلى القوة الوهمية المتأخرة عن مرتبتي القوتين

rows.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
rows.claim: Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya reads the people in whose chests whispering occurs as those forgetful of God in heart, secret, and spirit.
rows.anchor: أي الناسي ذكر الله بالقلب والسر والروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause is genitive as an adjective, so there is no pause after khannās; if read as accusative or nominative of censure, pausing there is acceptable.
rows.anchor: ومحل الموصول الجر على الوصف فلا وقف على الخناس أو النصب أو الرفع على الذم فيحسن الوقف عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chest is the heart’s vestibule: incoming influences gather there before entering the heart, while intentions and commands flow back through it to the body; Satan whispers in this passageway but reaches the heart.
rows.anchor: والصدر هو ساحة القلب وبيته فمنه تدخل الواردات عليه فتجتمع في الصدر ثم تلج في القلب فهو بمنزلة الدهليز

rows.speaker: أرباب الحقائق
rows.claim: Some masters of spiritual realities describe five outward, sensory commanders and five inward, spiritual commanders governing the heart; the list includes animal, imaginative, reflective, rational, and holy spirits.
rows.anchor: للقلب أمراء خمسة ملكية يسمون الحواس كحاسة البصر وحاسة السمع وحاسة الشم وحاسة الذوق وحاسة اللمس
